summary:
The Cook Islands is a self-governing state in free association with New Zealand. New Zealand nationality and passport rules apply to people of Cook Islands status, while local criminal law, the Cook Islands Crimes Act 1969 as amended, governs conduct on the islands.

Sexual activity between men is no longer an offence. Sections 154 and 155 of the 1969 Crimes Act criminalised sexual activity between men, carrying a maximum term of seven years, and any indecent act with or upon another male, carrying a maximum of five years, with consent expressly not a defence. Coverage of the 2023 repeal reported the exposure for indecent acts between males as high as ten years. The penalty figures differ across the sources; all of them agree that the provisions were never enforced.

Parliament voted on Friday 14 April 2023 to strike the provisions from the Crimes Act through the Crimes Amendment Bill, with the repeal effective 1 June 2023. A note attached to the bill cited growing acceptance of LGBT people in the Cook Islands.

The repeal was not a single-step event. A draft Crimes Bill prepared with New Zealand assistance in 2017 would have removed sections 154 and 155; a select committee that year recommended removing them, and the offences were struck from the draft, but members of parliament subsequently backtracked. In October 2020 the report stage of the Crimes Bill was deferred again, by three months, before the eventual 2023 passage.

The Crimes Amendment Bill that removed the offences also added protections for victims of sexual abuse and assault; the repeal of the male-conduct offences moved through parliament inside that wider package.

Same-sex marriage remains prohibited in the Cook Islands under the Marriage Amendment Act 2000.
tangentialFactors:
Colonisation is identified in the sourced material as the origin of the stigma the 1969 provisions attached to sex between men; the sources describe the society as historically more accepting of same-sex relationships before that period.

The legislative history shows that reform of these provisions was repeatedly delayed inside a single parliament over six years, between the 2017 select committee recommendation and the 2023 vote, including a three-month deferral of the bill's report stage in 2020. A visitor should not treat the date of statutory text as evidence of a settled legislative consensus.

Reporting around the repeal also focused on the small scale of the jurisdiction, with a population reported at about 21,000 in 2017, and on the role of the country's only LGBTI community group, the Te Tiare Association, which welcomed the 2017 draft and publicly condemned the law's homophobia.

Because the repeal was carried in a bill whose main subject was protections for victims of sexual abuse and assault, the removal of the offences has no separate explanatory record of its own beyond a note on shifting social acceptance.
localsOnly:
Public submissions on the Cook Islands Crimes Bill were opened in parliament in August 2017, with the clerk of Parliament confirming that a submission from the Te Tiare Association, representing the LGBTI community, was already before the select committee, alongside expected evidence from at least three lawyers on penalties and sentencing.

The Marriage Amendment Act 2000 continues to bar same-sex marriage for residents as well as visitors.

The law's repeal followed sustained local advocacy rather than external direction; the 2017 bill was drafted with New Zealand help, but the deferrals between 2017 and 2023 were taken by Cook Islands members of parliament.
outOfScopeNotes:
No source in the current inventory addresses legal gender recognition, change of name or gender markers on identity documents and passports, entry or border screening, access to gender-affirming health care, single-sex facilities, hate-crime or non-discrimination protection, or any other trans-specific legal question in the Cook Islands. The material documents only the decriminalisation of sexual conduct between men. Anything the record says about trans visitors' legal position is therefore unresolved, not settled either way.

The maximum penalties attached to sections 154 and 155 are reported inconsistently, as seven and five years in earlier coverage and as high as ten years in 2023 coverage of the repeal. Which figure corresponded to which provision at the time of repeal is unresolved in the sources.

Whether marriages or partnerships legally formed outside the Cook Islands are recognised for a same-sex couple under the Marriage Amendment Act 2000 is not sourced.

Whether any enforcement practice, informal or otherwise, accompanied the never-enforced provisions before 1 June 2023, and how the added sexual-abuse and assault protections are applied in practice, are not sourced.
